title: The theology of the cross
hookLine: Luther: God is found in weakness and suffering, not in glory

cards: Where would someone go looking for God? A mountain at sunrise, maybe. A cathedral full of music.

A winning streak that seems to say, someone up there is on my side. Martin Luther gave a sharp answer, and it wasn't any of those. The place to look, he said, is a man dying on a cross: mocked, abandoned and weak.
Speaking at a gathering of his own religious order, he drew a line between two kinds of theologian: a theologian of glory, and a theologian of the cross.

teach.b: A theologian of glory, Luther said, tries to read God off the world's strength: power, success, splendor, whatever impresses. It sounds reasonable.

But it ends up calling evil good and good evil, because it can't see God anywhere that looks like failure. A theologian of the cross calls a thing what it actually is. He looks at Good Friday and says: there.
God is there, hidden in suffering and weakness.

teach.h: THE WEAKNESS OF GOD IS STRONGER.
teach.b: Luther took his lead from Paul: "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men."
Paul had begged to be rid of something he called a thorn in the flesh, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
In the disputation itself, Luther also points to a line from Isaiah: "Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself." So in Luther's picture, God isn't missing from the hard places.
God is hidden in them, on purpose, where people don't think to look. Then a hospital room looks different. So does a business that failed, or a body that won't heal.
A theologian of glory asks, what did I do wrong to end up here? A theologian of the cross asks, is God here too? Luther doesn't call suffering good in itself.
He says God meets people inside it. Christians who keep a crucifix in sight, or who sit up with the dying, are saying something close to this without a word of theology.

how: Lutheran Christians, and others who draw on Luther, speak of the theology of the cross in preaching and pastoral care; across churches, Christians keep the crucifix or cross in view and visit the sick and dying as places where Christ is met.

games.q: what does “the theology of the cross” mean?
o: Luther's teaching that God is found hidden in weakness
the history of the cross as a Roman punishment
the study of crosses and other Christian symbols

games.q: God hidden in weakness — tap the pairs.
p: reads God off power and success
calls a thing what it is

s: Luther taught that suffering is good in itself
he said God meets people in suffering, hidden there, not that suffering is good.
Paul heard "my strength is made perfect in weakness"
2 Corinthians 12:9, after he begged to be rid of a thorn in the flesh.
a theologian of glory finds God most easily in failure
the theologian of glory reads God off power and success, and can't see God where things look like failure.

games.q: two theologians look at Good Friday. one says: God is far from this failure. the other says: God is right here. which one is Luther's theologian of the cross?
o: the one who says God is far away.
the one who says God is right here, hidden in weakness.
neither: Good Friday says nothing about God.
games.why: the theologian of the cross calls a thing what it is, and finds God hidden in suffering and weakness, at the cross above all.

practice: Bring to mind one weak place, a fear or failure of your own, or a friend who is sick or struggling, and look at it honestly without rushing to fix it. Then ask quietly: could God be here too? If you pray, ask it of God directly.

wordCard.voice: The theology of the cross. Luther's teaching that God is found hidden in weakness and suffering, above all at the cross, not read off the world's glory.

orig.note: Greek, weakness, the word in 2 Corinthians 12:9: strength made perfect in weakness.

carryVoice: Your line: God hidden in weakness. For Luther, the cross is where to look. Go gently.
